I have been building AI systems for eight years, so people often ask me to predict the future. Here is my honest view. In five years, most companies will be using AI assistants that read and summarize documents. That part is almost certain. By then, these systems will have learned to write quotes and standard emails in many languages, very well. They will be faster than any human. But there is one thing they will not have learned, in my opinion: to take responsibility. If a machine makes a mistake in a contract, who signs it? Who answers to the client? A person. So my advice to business owners is: use the machine, but keep the signature.

Every time a new technology arrives, people predict the end of work. When spreadsheets appeared in the eighties, everybody said accountants would disappear. Today there are more accountants than ever; they just do different things. I think AI will be similar. By 2035, it will have changed almost every office job, but it won't have eliminated most of them. People will be doing less routine work and more of the things machines are bad at: talking to clients, negotiating, making decisions with incomplete information. And the most valuable skill? Asking good questions, and knowing when the answer is wrong.

When the first AI summaries appeared, I was worried. I thought, in ten years nobody will be reading full books anymore. But something interesting has happened. In our company, readers who use summaries are actually buying more full books, not fewer. The summary works like a trailer. It helps people choose. So I'm optimistic. By the end of this decade, machines will have summarized every book ever written, probably. But a summary will never give you the experience of reading: the voice of the author, the time you spend with the book, the sentence that stays with you for years. That is something you have to do yourself.
